title: Navigating Trade-Offs, Can We Leave Curriculum Behind? lum-behind/
author: Clare Stoneman
summary: Clare Stoneman, a school principal, warns against letting the current enthusiasm for generic instructional-coaching 'moves and steps' push curriculum content into the background. While she credits a shared vocabulary and set of learning principles with transforming teaching quality at her school since 2022, she argues coaching cannot be divorced from subject content: citing David Didau's line that 'we cannot think with or about something we don't know,' she insists coaches must be genuine subject specialists, not generalists with a passing familiarity with a curriculum overview. Her practical stance is that schools face real opportunity costs in how they spend professional-development time, but curriculum knowledge itself should never be treated as the trade-off sacrificed for generic pedagogical technique.
points: Stoneman's central warning: an insistence on generic instructional-coaching moves and steps risks treating curriculum as an optional trade-off -- 'Do not make curriculum a trade-off. I repeat: do not make curriculum a trade-off.'
She credits a shared vocabulary and common 'principles of learning' with driving a genuine, measurable shift in teaching quality at her school since becoming principal in September 2022.

Citing David Didau's Making Kids Cleverer, she argues effective coaching requires genuine subject expertise -- 'we cannot think with or about something we don't know' -- not a superficial scan of a curriculum overview.

Her practical conclusion: schools genuinely face opportunity costs in how PD time is spent, but pedagogy must always stay explicitly linked to subject content rather than treated as a generic, content-agnostic skill set.
quotes: Has curriculum had its day, peaked, and troughed? Are we back to the days of pedagogy (and what do we even mean by ‘pedagogy’?) as the be-all and the end-all? Let’s hope not. Because pedagogy should always be in service of curriculum.
Do not make curriculum a trade-off. I repeat: do not make curriculum a trade-off. For to overly (or only) focus on pedagogy is a thoughtless, cloth-eared error.
If the teacher and coach don’t know the content that’s being taught well enough, no instructional coaching – directional or facilitative – will work.
In Making Kids Cleverer, David Didau says that, 'We cannot think with or about something we don't know.'

To know more about a subject’s curriculum doesn’t mean a quick read through the curriculum overview or a cursory scan through the latest subject edu-book lobbed into an Amazon basket. That’s a knowledge chimera, an illusion.
